lesson.title: Demodulation: Pulling the Data Back Out of the Carrier
lesson.summary: Demodulation is the receiver side inverse of modulation: it strips a transmitted carrier wave back down to the bits or waveform it was carrying, which is what makes radios, modems, and Wi-Fi receivers actually useful.
lesson.body:
Modulation, as you saw earlier, takes a signal you want to send and uses it to vary some property of a carrier wave, its amplitude, frequency, or phase, so that the data can travel efficiently over a channel that is not well suited to the raw baseband signal. Demodulation is the necessary mirror image of that process. At the receiving end, a demodulator examines the incoming carrier and reconstructs the original variations, recovering the bits or analog signal that the transmitter started with. Without demodulation, modulation would be a one way trick: you could shape a signal for transmission, but nobody on the other end could get the message back out.

The mechanics of demodulation depend directly on which property the modulator varied. If the transmitter used amplitude shift keying (ASK), the receiver can use an envelope detector, a simple circuit that tracks the peak amplitude of the incoming wave over time and compares it to a threshold. If the transmitter used frequency shift keying (FSK), the demodulator instead measures which of two or more frequencies is present during each symbol interval, often with a bank of filters or a frequency discriminator. Phase shift keying (PSK) and quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) are harder still: the receiver needs a locally generated reference wave synchronized in frequency and phase with the transmitter's carrier, typically produced by a phase locked loop, so it can measure how far the incoming signal's phase has shifted relative to that reference.

Consider a concrete case: a transmitter using ASK to send the bits 1, 0, 1, 1 over a fixed frequency carrier. It sends the carrier at full amplitude for a 1 and at near zero amplitude for a 0, one bit per symbol interval. At the receiver, an envelope detector tracks the amplitude of the incoming wave and a comparator samples that envelope once per symbol period, right in the middle where the reading is most stable. Reading full amplitude, near zero, full amplitude, full amplitude across four consecutive samples, the demodulator outputs exactly the sequence 1, 0, 1, 1, reconstructing the transmitted bits without ever seeing them directly, only inferring them from the shape of the wave.

Real channels complicate this. Noise added along the way can push an amplitude reading, a frequency estimate, or a phase measurement just far enough to be misread, so demodulators are built with filtering and averaging to reject noise before it reaches the decision stage. Timing matters just as much: the demodulator has to know exactly where each symbol interval begins and ends to sample at the right instant, a synchronization problem that real systems solve with recovered clock signals or known preamble patterns sent at the start of a transmission.

It is worth noting that demodulation is specifically about recovering a signal from a modulated carrier wave. When data instead travels as a baseband digital signal with no carrier involved, the analogous receive side task is called decoding, which you will look at once you have seen how digital signals are encoded onto a physical medium in the first place. The device that performs both modulation and demodulation on a single line, letting two computers exchange data over a channel built for something else, like a telephone circuit, is exactly what a modem, short for modulator demodulator, was built to do.
